passage: Karthik, you've stopped telling your girlfriend about your marks, haven't you? I saw your face at lunch. Let your Pema Ani tell you something that happened to me. At twenty-one, in Darjeeling, I won a scholarship to study nursing in Delhi. I ran to tell Norbu, the boy I was seeing. He said, 'Delhi? Good, now you'll think you're too big for us,' laughed, and changed the subject. Every good thing after that, he had a joke ready. So I started hiding things. I didn't tell him when I topped the first term. I felt like I was shrinking myself to keep him comfortable. Then my sister said, 'Pema, why are you whispering your own news?' So I sat Norbu down and said, kindly, 'When you joke about my wins, it hurts. I want you to be happy for me.' He tried for a while. It didn't last, and we parted. But I never whispered my good news again.

qa.q: What did Norbu say when Pema told him about the scholarship?
qa.a: 'Delhi? Good, now you'll think you're too big for us.'

qa.q: How did Pema feel hiding her first-term result?
qa.a: She felt small, as if shrinking herself to keep Norbu comfortable.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Pema's story?
qa.a: Her sister asking why she whispered her own news, which led Pema to talk kindly but honestly with Norbu.

qa.q: How might Norbu have felt about Pema's scholarship?
qa.a: Probably envious and insecure, afraid she would outgrow him, which came out as jokes.

grounding: An elder's story of good news met with cold jokes, noticing it, talking kindly, and refusing to hide success to protect a partner's ego.

passage: Gurleen got the offer letter at noon: a design job at a studio she'd dreamed about since first year. By one o'clock she had told Chetan, who had been rejected by three firms that month. 'Nice,' he texted. Just that. At his cousin's engagement party that evening, loud with dhol and relatives, someone congratulated her, and Chetan said, 'Yeah, she's the famous one now. I just carry her bags.' People laughed. Gurleen's cheeks burned. She almost played it down: 'It's only a junior role.' She stopped herself. Outside, by the parked cars, she said quietly, 'Chetan, that joke hurt. I know this month's been awful for you, and I'm sorry. But I'm not going to hide good news to make things easier.' He looked at his shoes. 'I'm jealous. I hate that I'm jealous.' 'Then tell me that, not the room.' Later that night she called her best friend, who screamed with joy down the phone. Gurleen let herself feel it fully.

qa.q: What did Chetan say at the engagement party?
qa.a: 'Yeah, she's the famous one now. I just carry her bags.'

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel when people laughed at the joke?
qa.a: Her cheeks burned with hurt and embarrassment.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do instead of playing down her news?
qa.a: She told Chetan kindly that the joke hurt, refused to hide her success, and celebrated with a friend who cheered.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling underneath the joke?
qa.a: Jealousy, after a month of rejections, which he admits and hates feeling.

grounding: Shows a young woman whose good news is met with a cold joke, talking kindly with her partner and celebrating with someone who cheers instead of hiding it.

passage:
Shreya's phone buzzed on the table while she was in the kitchen. Deepak saw the name: Aman. Third time today. His hand actually moved towards the phone. He pulled it back.
When she came out with two bowls of instant noodles, he said, 'Can I ask something without it sounding bad?'
'That's a scary start.'
'I've been feeling suspicious, and I hate it. You've been texting Aman a lot. I nearly looked at your phone just now. I didn't.'
Shreya put the bowls down slowly. 'Thank you for not looking. And for asking.' She unlocked the phone and held it out. He shook his head.
'I don't want to read it. I want to hear it.'
'Aman's organising the surprise for my sister's graduation. I've been hiding it from her, not from you.'
Deepak let out a long breath. 'My brain made a whole movie out of three texts.'
'Next time, ask sooner. Movies are worse than questions.'

qa.q: Who is Aman, according to Shreya?
qa.a: The person organising the surprise for her sister's graduation.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when the phone buzzed?
qa.a: He felt suspicious and anxious, enough that his hand moved towards her phone.

qa.q: What did Deepak do instead of spying?
qa.a: He pulled his hand back and calmly told Shreya his worry, asking to hear the truth rather than read her phone 👍

qa.q: How does Shreya respond to Deepak's question?
qa.a: She thanks him for not looking and for asking, and explains openly.

grounding: Shows a young man whose suspicion rises over a partner's texts, separating anxiety from evidence and asking calmly instead of checking her phone.

passage: Last winter I did something I'm still ashamed of. I'm Lalremsiami, Siami to everyone, and my boyfriend Kishore had started liking every photo a new girl in his office posted. Then his replies got slower. My mind raced: late nights, new friend, likes. One night, while he was in the shower, I unlocked his phone and read his chats. There was nothing. Office jokes, a group chat about a football match, messages to his mum. I sat on the bed feeling sick, not relieved, because I'd just done the very thing I'd hate to have done to me. When he came out, I told him. He was quiet and hurt. 'You could have just asked me.' He was right. What I had was anxiety left over from my last relationship, not evidence. We talked for a long time that night. Now, when the doubt starts, I write down what I actually know, and then I ask him. Calmly. It's worked every time so far.

qa.q: What did Siami find on Kishore's phone?
qa.a: Nothing worrying: office jokes, a football group chat, messages to his mum.

qa.q: How did Siami feel after reading the chats?
qa.a: Siami felt sick and ashamed rather than relieved, having done something that would hurt if done in return.

qa.q: What does Siami do now when doubt starts?
qa.a: Writes down what is actually known, then asks Kishore calmly.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel when he learned about the phone?
qa.a: Quiet and hurt, wishing Siami had just asked him.

grounding: A first-person account of suspicion leading to secretly checking a partner's phone, then learning to separate anxiety from evidence and ask calmly.

passage: Noor, you keep saying sorry for things you didn't do. Come, sit with your Irawati Aunty for a minute. When I was twenty-one, I was engaged to a man named Sameer. At first he was sweet. Then the questions started. 'Why were you late from college? Who was that on the phone? Why did you smile at the vegetable seller?' I would explain calmly, with facts. The bus was late. It was my sister. The vegetable seller is sixty. He'd believe me for a day, then accuse me of something new. I began to think maybe I was doing something wrong, maybe I was a bad person. My mother noticed I'd stopped laughing. She said, 'Ira, look at the pattern, not the latest question. Does it ever end?' It didn't. I ended the engagement. The family was upset for a year. I have never once regretted it. Suspicion that never stops isn't your guilt, beta. It's a warning.

qa.q: Who was actually on the phone, according to Irawati?
qa.a: Her sister.

qa.q: How had Irawati started to feel under the constant accusations?
qa.a: She began to doubt herself, feeling guilty and wondering if she was a bad person.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Irawati's story?
qa.a: Her mother telling her to look at the pattern, not the latest question, which led her to end the engagement.

qa.q: How did Irawati's mother see the situation?
qa.a: She noticed Irawati had stopped laughing and saw the endless suspicion as the real problem.

grounding: An elder's story of being constantly accused without cause, staying calm with facts, and recognising never-ending suspicion as a warning sign.

passage: It was the night before Swati's final practical exam, and Gopika had called four times. 'Why were you online at eleven? Who were you talking to?' 'My lab group, about the titration steps,' Swati said, steady. 'I can send you the screenshot.' 'You always have a screenshot ready. That's suspicious in itself.' Swati closed her notes. It was the third accusation this week. Last Monday it was a classmate's birthday post; on Thursday, a late bus. Each time she'd stated the facts calmly, and each time a new question arrived. She had started apologising for things she hadn't done. Sitting on the hostel floor, she did what her counsellor had suggested and listed the week's accusations. Six. None true. None ended. 'Gopika,' she said, 'I've answered every question honestly. I can't keep proving I'm innocent. I think we need to talk about this after my exam, maybe with a counsellor.' Then she switched her phone to silent and slept.

qa.q: How many accusations were on Swati's list for the week?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: How did Swati feel after a week of accusations?
qa.a: She had started feeling guilty and apologising for things she hadn't done.

qa.q: What steps did Swati take to protect herself?
qa.a: Stated facts calmly, listed the accusations to see the pattern, proposed talking with a counsellor, and silenced her phone to sleep.

qa.q: What might Gopika's constant suspicion suggest?
qa.a: Gopika's own insecurity, which is a warning sign rather than proof of Swati's guilt.

grounding: Shows a young woman repeatedly accused without cause, staying calm with facts and recognising unending suspicion as a warning sign.

passage: In a Sector 17 café in Chandigarh, Sumit's phone lit up with a message from Riddhi, his ex, congratulating him on his internship. Baljeet saw the name and felt the old knot tighten. She had already asked him, more than once, how long they'd dated, why they broke up, whether Riddhi was prettier. Last month, in an argument about something else entirely, she'd thrown it at him: 'Maybe you'd rather be with Riddhi.' She remembered his face then. Now she held her tea and made herself breathe. The past wasn't a threat; Sumit had chosen her every day for a year. 'Can I be honest about something?' she said. 'When her name comes up, I get scared I'm a replacement. It's not about anything you've done. And I'm sorry I used it in that fight.' Sumit reached across the table. 'You're not a replacement. Thank you for saying it like that instead of asking twenty questions.' The knot loosened.

qa.q: What did Riddhi congratulate Sumit on?
qa.a: His internship.

qa.q: What was Baljeet afraid of when Riddhi's name came up?
qa.a: She was scared of being a replacement, a jealous fear rooted in the past.

qa.q: What did Baljeet do differently this time?
qa.a: She named the fear honestly, apologised for using it in a fight, and didn't interrogate him.

qa.q: How did Sumit respond to Baljeet's honesty?
qa.a: He reassured her she isn't a replacement and thanked her for sharing it without twenty questions.

grounding: Shows a young woman jealous of her partner's ex, accepting the past isn't a threat and talking about the fear instead of interrogating or using it as a weapon.

passage:
'You still have photos with him on your profile,' Saurabh said, trying to sound casual. 'From Goa. Three years ago.'
Madhuri looked up from her laptop. 'Rahul? Yeah. I never went back and deleted anything.'
'Why not? Do you still...'
He stopped. He could hear himself building up to twenty questions.
'Still what?'
Saurabh sat on the arm of the sofa. 'Sorry. Let me start again. When I saw those photos, I felt jealous. And scared. Like I'm competing with someone who isn't even here.'
'You're not competing with anyone. That was a different time, a different me.'
'I know. My brain doesn't always know it.'
'Do you want me to delete them?'
He thought about it. 'No. That's your history. I don't want you erasing it for me. I just wanted to tell you the fear instead of fighting about the photos.'
Madhuri smiled. 'That's the most grown-up thing you've said all month.'
'Don't get used to it.'

qa.q: Where were the old photos with Rahul taken?
qa.a: In Goa, three years ago.

qa.q: What did Saurabh feel seeing the photos?
qa.a: He felt jealous and scared, as if competing with someone who wasn't even there.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do instead of interrogating Madhuri?
qa.a: He stopped himself mid-question and named his fear honestly, without asking her to erase her past.

qa.q: How does Madhuri see the photos?
qa.a: As a different time and a different version of herself, not a threat.

grounding: Shows a young man jealous of his partner's ex, stopping an interrogation and talking about the fear while accepting her past.

passage: Dhruv was on the metro to Indiranagar when the photo came up: Jyoti, laughing on a beach in Gokarna, arm around a tall guy in a red cap. Four months since she'd ended things. The sting was sharp and physical, like missing a step. By the time he reached his stop, he had opened the guy's profile, counted his followers, and drafted a story of himself at a rooftop party, just to show he was fine. He stood on the platform with his thumb over 'post'. Then he thought: who is this for? Not for him. It was for Jyoti to see, and maybe to sting her back. He deleted the draft. He muted Jyoti and the man in the red cap and put the phone away. At home he called his friend Aakash and admitted, 'It hurts more than I thought.' Aakash said, 'It will, for a while. Her being happy doesn't mean you weren't enough.' Dhruv sat with that. It helped a little.

qa.q: Where was Jyoti in the photo?
qa.a: On a beach in Gokarna.

qa.q: What did Dhruv feel when he saw the photo?
qa.a: A sharp, physical sting of jealousy and hurt, like missing a step.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do instead of posting to provoke?
qa.a: He deleted the draft, muted Jyoti and her new partner, and called Aakash to admit the hurt.

qa.q: How does Aakash see Jyoti's new happiness?
qa.a: As no verdict on Dhruv; her being happy doesn't mean he wasn't enough.

grounding: Shows a young man stung by his ex's new partner, resisting comparison and provocation, muting them and letting the pain pass.

passage:
'He's here with her,' Vasudha whispered, gripping Maria's arm at the college fest. Across the lawn, her ex, Kunal, was sharing a plate of momos with a girl in a green kurta.
'Okay. Breathe,' Maria said. 'Want to leave?'
'No. Yes. I don't know.' Vasudha's eyes were stinging. 'She's so pretty. What does she have that I didn't?'
'Stop right there. This isn't a competition.'
'I'm going to message her. Just to say hi. Just to see.'
'Vasu. Just to see what? To make her uncomfortable? To make him notice you?'
Vasudha stared at her phone. 'Maybe.'
'Then no. You'd hate yourself tomorrow.'
Vasudha put the phone away, slowly. 'It really hurts.'
'I know. Let it hurt. It'll pass. And him being happy doesn't mean you weren't worth it.'
'Can we get chaat on the other side of the fest?'
'And mute him on the way.'
'Both. Yes.'

qa.q: What was Kunal sharing with the girl in the green kurta?
qa.a: A plate of momos.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she saw Kunal with someone new?
qa.a: Her eyes stung with hurt and jealousy, and she compared herself to the new girl.

qa.q: How did Maria help Vasudha avoid a mistake?
qa.a: She asked what messaging the new girl was really for, and steered Vasudha to let it hurt, mute Kunal and go for chaat.

qa.q: How might the girl in the green kurta feel if Vasudha had messaged her?
qa.a: Probably uncomfortable and confused, pulled into something that wasn't about her.

grounding: Shows a young woman stung by her ex's new partner, choosing not to compare or contact her, and letting the pain pass with a friend.

passage: Ada had been best friends with Tomasz since primary school in Leeds, long before Emeka came along. They had inside jokes Emeka didn't understand, a Friday film night, and a way of finishing each other's sentences that made his stomach tighten. Twice he'd almost said, 'Maybe you should see less of him.' He knew how that would land: as an order. So one Sunday, walking back from the market, he said instead, 'Can I tell you something a bit embarrassing? I feel insecure about Tomasz. It's not anything he's done. You two just have so much history.' Ada squeezed his arm. 'Thank you for telling me. Why don't you come to film night?' He went. Tomasz had made terrible popcorn and an even worse pun about it. By the end of the evening the two of them were arguing happily about football. Walking home, Emeka realised the unease had shrunk to something small and ordinary.

qa.q: How long had Ada and Tomasz been best friends?
qa.a: Since primary school in Leeds.

qa.q: What was Emeka feeling about Ada and Tomasz's closeness?
qa.a: He felt insecure, his stomach tightening at their shared history and inside jokes.

qa.q: What did Emeka do instead of asking Ada to see less of Tomasz?
qa.a: He shared his feeling honestly and then got to know Tomasz at film night.

qa.q: How does Ada respond to Emeka's confession?
qa.a: She thanks him and invites him to film night, including him rather than defending herself 😊

grounding: Shows a young man uneasy about his partner's close male friend, sharing the feeling and getting to know him instead of ordering distance.

passage: At the university research lab where they all worked, Ujjwal's girlfriend Anjali spent long afternoons at the next bench with Tenzin, her project partner and closest friend from undergrad. They shared earphones while running experiments and laughed at pipette jokes nobody else found funny. Ujjwal, working two rooms away, felt a knot of unease every time he passed the glass door. One evening he drafted a message: 'Either you switch partners or we need to talk.' He looked at it for a long time. It was an ultimatum, and he knew it. He deleted it. At the lab's Friday tea, he pulled up a stool next to Tenzin instead and asked about the project. Tenzin turned out to be shy, obsessed with mountain birds, and planning to propose to his own girlfriend in Sikkim. Later Ujjwal told Anjali, 'I've been feeling insecure about you two. Talking to him helped.' She hugged him. 'Thank you for not making me choose.'

qa.q: What is Tenzin obsessed with?
qa.a: Mountain birds.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal feel each time he passed the glass door?
qa.a: A knot of unease and insecurity about Anjali's closeness with Tenzin.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do instead of sending the ultimatum?
qa.a: He deleted it, got to know Tenzin at Friday tea, and then shared his feeling honestly with Anjali.

qa.q: How does Anjali respond when Ujjwal tells her?
qa.a: She hugs him, grateful he didn't make her choose.

grounding: Shows a young man insecure about his partner's close male friend, rejecting an ultimatum, getting to know him and sharing the feeling honestly.

passage: You asked what the worst week of my life was. Honestly, this one. I'm Ritu, and on Monday I found out Jatin had been seeing someone else for three months. I saw the messages on his laptop when he asked me to print his assignment. First I felt nothing, as if my body had switched off. Then rage, so much that I wanted to post the screenshots everywhere and message the girl. Then, strangely, shame, as if I was the stupid one for not noticing. By Wednesday I was sure it was my fault: not pretty enough, too busy with exams. My roommate Meenal sat with me on the floor and said, 'Ritu, he chose to lie. That was his choice, not your flaw.' I haven't posted anything. I haven't decided anything about us either. I told Jatin I need two weeks of no contact before we even talk. I'm going home to my sister this weekend. I'm leaning on people. That's all I can do right now.

qa.q: How did Ritu find out about Jatin?
qa.a: By seeing the messages on Jatin's laptop while printing his assignment.

qa.q: What feelings did Ritu go through during the week?
qa.a: Ritu felt numb, then furious, then ashamed, and by Wednesday was full of self-doubt and self-blame.

qa.q: What did Ritu choose to do instead of revenge?
qa.a: Asked for two weeks of no contact, didn't post the screenshots, and leaned on Meenal and a sister.

qa.q: How does Meenal see what happened?
qa.a: As Jatin's choice to lie, not a flaw in Ritu.

grounding: A spoken account of discovering a partner's cheating, feeling shock, rage and shame, and taking time and leaning on friends instead of revenge or self-blame.

passage: Saturday. Vasudha found out from a mutual friend's careless story: her boyfriend Aman at a café in Pune with another girl, his hand on hers, on the night he'd said he was studying. She rang him. He admitted it. She hung up and sat on the hostel stairs, shaking, unable to cry. Jyoti found her there at midnight and didn't leave. Tuesday. Rage had arrived. Vasudha drafted a long post naming him, then a message to the other girl. Jyoti read both and said, 'Write them. Don't send them.' Vasudha deleted them. She also caught herself asking, 'What's wrong with me that he did this?' 'Nothing,' Jyoti said. 'He made a choice.' Two weeks later. Vasudha still hadn't decided whether she would ever talk to Aman again, and she was letting that be okay. She'd been to the counselling centre once. She was eating properly again. Some mornings she still woke up heavy. But she had stopped blaming herself.

qa.q: How did Vasudha find out about Aman?
qa.a: From a mutual friend's careless story showing him at a café in Pune with another girl.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling on the hostel stairs that Saturday?
qa.a: She was in shock, shaking and unable to cry.

qa.q: How did Vasudha handle the urge for revenge?
qa.a: With Jyoti's help she wrote the post and message but deleted them instead of sending.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see Aman's cheating?
qa.a: As his choice, not a sign that something is wrong with Vasudha.

grounding: Shows a young woman who discovers her partner's cheating, moving through shock and rage with a friend's support, avoiding revenge and self-blame, and taking time.

passage:
Dear Nazia,
I'm writing because I owe you the truth in full, not in pieces.
At the conference in Hyderabad last month, I kissed someone. It happened on the last night. In the moment I felt a rush, as if I were someone new. By morning I felt sick, and I've felt sick every day since. I lied to you on the phone when you asked how the trip was. That was the second betrayal.
I've thought about why. It isn't because of anything you did. I've been feeling lost about my career, and I went looking for a thrill instead of talking to you. That's on me, completely.
I've ended all contact with her. I'm not asking you to forgive me, and I'm not asking you to decide anything soon. Whatever you choose, I'll accept it. If you want to talk, I'll be there. If you don't, I'll understand.
I'm so sorry.
Lokesh

qa.q: Where did Lokesh cross the line?
qa.a: At the conference in Hyderabad, on the last night.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel the morning after?
qa.a: Lokesh felt sick with guilt, and has felt that dread every day since.

qa.q: What does Lokesh do right in this letter?
qa.a: Admits the full truth, owns the reason without blaming Nazia, ends contact, and accepts whatever Nazia decides.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Likely hurt and shocked, but at least told the whole truth rather than lied to further.

grounding: A letter from a young person who cheated, feeling a thrill then guilt, admitting it fully, ending the deception and accepting the consequences without blame.

passage: Eshaan, you're the only one I can say this to. I'm Deepak, and I cheated on Kavya. There, it's out. It started as texting a girl from my gym. It felt exciting, like being in a film. Then we met twice. The first week I felt this buzz. The second week I couldn't sleep. When Kavya asked why I was always on my phone, I lied. When she pushed, I snapped: 'You're so busy with your MBA, what did you expect?' I actually said that. Blamed her for my choice. Then I went home and sat with it. It wasn't her MBA. It was me wanting to feel wanted without doing the work of telling her I felt ignored. So yesterday I told her everything. No excuses. I ended it with the girl from the gym. Kavya cried and asked me to leave. I want her to forgive me so badly. But I don't get to demand that. I just have to live with what I did, and be honest from here.

qa.q: Where did Deepak meet the girl he texted?
qa.a: At his gym.

qa.q: What did Deepak feel in the second week?
qa.a: He felt guilty and full of dread, unable to sleep after the first week's thrill.

qa.q: What did Deepak eventually do right?
qa.a: He told Kavya everything without excuses, ended the other relationship, and accepted that he can't demand forgiveness.

qa.q: How did Kavya respond when Deepak told her?
qa.a: She cried and asked him to leave.

grounding: A spoken account of a young man who cheated, first blaming his partner and lying, then confessing honestly, ending it and accepting the consequences.

passage:
Dear Vandana Didi,
You asked if I've forgiven Rohit yet. The honest answer is: I don't know, and I'm learning that's allowed.
It's been two months since I found out. He has done everything he said he would: told me the full truth, ended contact with her, started counselling, and answered every hard question without getting defensive. Some days I look at him and feel the old warmth. Other days a cold wave hits and I have to leave the room.
Last week I almost said 'I forgive you' just because I was so tired of being sad, and scared of coming home to an empty flat. I stopped myself. That wouldn't be forgiveness. That would be loneliness talking.
So I've told him I need more time, maybe months. I'm watching what he does, not what he promises. And if the trust doesn't come back, leaving is a valid choice too, not a failure.
Call me Sunday?
Sunaina

qa.q: How long has it been since Sunaina found out?
qa.a: Two months.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina almost say 'I forgive you'?
qa.a: Sunaina felt tired of being sad and scared of the loneliness of an empty flat.

qa.q: What is Sunaina's approach to forgiveness now?
qa.a: Taking more time, watching Rohit's changed behaviour rather than promises, and accepting that leaving is also valid.

qa.q: How has Rohit responded since being found out?
qa.a: He told the full truth, cut contact, started counselling and answers hard questions without getting defensive.

grounding: A letter from a young person unsure whether to forgive a partner's betrayal, refusing forced or lonely forgiveness and giving it time.

passage: Ishita, people keep asking me why I didn't give Varun another chance. So I'll tell you properly, once. I'm Swati. When I found out he'd been cheating, he begged. Flowers, long letters, 'I'll change'. My mum said good men make mistakes. And I wanted to believe him, honestly, because the idea of starting over scared me. So I tried. For three months. But every time I asked a question, he got angry, as if I was punishing him. He kept 'forgetting' to tell me where he was. The apology didn't match what he actually did. One night I realised I was staying because I was afraid of being alone, not because I trusted him. That's not forgiveness. That's fear. So I ended it. I cried for weeks. But I don't regret it. Forgiving him in my heart, maybe one day. Staying? That was my choice to make, and walking away was valid too.

qa.q: How long did Swati try after finding out?
qa.a: Three months.

qa.q: What did Swati realise one night?
qa.a: Swati realised the staying came from being afraid of loneliness, not from trust.

qa.q: Why was walking away a valid choice for Swati?
qa.a: Varun's behaviour didn't change, and forgiveness can't be forced; leaving was as valid as staying.

qa.q: How did Swati's mum see the situation?
qa.a: She believed good men make mistakes and hoped for forgiveness.

grounding: A spoken account of trying to forgive a cheating partner, noticing that staying was fear of loneliness without changed behaviour, and choosing to walk away.

passage: Week one. After the kiss at the office farewell, Dilnaz couldn't eat. Every time Aadhya smiled at her across the dinner table, guilt burned. She wanted to blurt it out just to make the feeling stop. Week two. At 1 a.m. she shook Aadhya awake to confess, then stopped halfway. Was she about to tell Aadhya for Aadhya's sake, or so she could cry and be comforted? She lay back down, shaken by the answer. The next day she talked to a counsellor. They discussed what honesty would serve: Aadhya's right to know and to choose, yes; Dilnaz's relief, no. And she had to be ready to lose everything. Week four. Dilnaz told Aadhya on a Sunday afternoon, calmly, not at midnight. She said what had happened, took full responsibility, and didn't ask for comfort. 'You don't have to decide anything. And you don't have to look after me.' Aadhya went to her sister's that night. Dilnaz let her go.

qa.q: Where did the kiss happen?
qa.a: At the office farewell.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz feel when Aadhya smiled across the dinner table?
qa.a: Burning guilt, strong enough that Dilnaz couldn't eat.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz change about how she confessed?
qa.a: She waited, reflected with a counsellor, and told Aadhya calmly in the afternoon, taking full responsibility without asking to be comforted.

qa.q: How did Aadhya respond to the confession?
qa.a: She went to her sister's that night.

grounding: Shows a young woman eaten by guilt after cheating, questioning whether confession serves her partner or just her own relief, and confessing without making her guilt her partner's burden.

passage: Bhupen, I hear you're thinking of telling Rimi something at 2 a.m. to 'get it off your chest'. Let your old Jagdish Kaka tell you what I did at your age, and what I wish I'd done. At twenty-one, engaged to a girl from our village, I went to a friend's wedding in Guwahati and spent a night with someone else. I came back sick with guilt. One night I woke my fiancée and confessed, crying, and then begged her to tell me I was still a good person. She sat up till dawn comforting me. Me! The one who'd hurt her. Only years later did I see what I'd done: I'd made my guilt her job. So listen, beta. If you tell Rimi, tell her because she deserves the truth and the choice. Tell her in daylight, calmly. Take the responsibility yourself. And don't ask her to hold your guilt. That part is yours to carry.

qa.q: Where was the wedding Jagdish went to?
qa.a: A friend's wedding in Guwahati.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when he came back from the wedding?
qa.a: He felt sick with guilt.

qa.q: What turning point does Jagdish describe in his story?
qa.a: Realising years later that confessing at night and begging for comfort had made his guilt his fiancée's job.

qa.q: What was that night like for Jagdish's fiancée?
qa.a: She had to sit up till dawn comforting the person who had hurt her.

grounding: An elder's story of confessing infidelity to feel lighter and making his partner comfort him, and advice to confess only for her sake and carry the guilt himself.
